newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin refuses to lay Lenin burial idea to rest.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin refuses to lay Lenin burial idea to rest.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday pressed on with the idea of giving Vladimir Lenin's mummified corpse a Christian burial, hinting that he might go ahead and do it without a referendum.

"I also throw this problem at you. How will you respond? Should the mausoleum be removed from Red Square...Shall we do that?" Yeltsin asked an audience of leading writers, artists and actors, who responded with applause.

"We will of course examine public opinion on this issue," Yeltsin went on. "But to turn Red Square into a cemetery -- No! That contradicts the laws of the church which say a dead person must be buried below the ground and not above it."

Yeltsin outraged his communist parliamentary opponents last Friday by suggesting that the people should decide what to do with the body of the atheist Bolshevik leader, which has lain on Red Square for 73 years.
The remarks coincided with a rise in tension between Yeltsin and parliament, which has criticised his government's tough budget plans and passed a bill saying Red Square should remain untouched.
Even liberal politicians criticised Yeltsin's idea, raised during a meeting of his Council on Culture and Art in St Petersburg -- part of a recent bid to woo the cultural elite.

They said Russia had more pressing problems and suggested that most Russians, brought up to consider Lenin a hero, might oppose destroying the monument to his genius, even though it is no longer a place of popular pilgrimage.
But Yeltsin, undeterred, used another meeting of the liberal intelligentsia to raise the issue, doubtless knowing in advance he could count on their approval.

His test of public opinion came suddenly in the middle of the awards ceremony. Extracts were broadcast on television news, driving home the message to viewers that the burial idea had the support of intellectuals, considered an influential force in Russia despite their fading fortunes.

Yeltsin, honing his image as the man who rid Russia of its communist past, also repeated an assertion he made in March that Lenin had written in his will that he wanted to be buried in St Petersburg alongside his mother.

But communists say the atheist leader did no such thing. "In the Russian state historical archives...we were told officially that no will by Lenin exists," the communist daily Pravda wrote on Saturday, adding that there was no evidence that he even told anyone what he wanted done with his body.

The paper said if Yeltsin wanted to concern himself with funerals he should concentrate on finding and reburying the missing bodies of Russian soldiers killed in World War Two and in his ill-fated campaign in Chechnya which ended last year.
